articles.title: Dana Carvey Doesn’t ‘Understand the Kerfuffle’ Over Shane Gillis’ ‘Whores’ Joke: ‘Did I Just Get Canceled?’
articles.summary: Dana Carvey became the latest "Saturday Night Live" figure to weigh in on host Shane Gillis' controversial joke about women.
articles.body:
Dana Carvey became the latest "Saturday Night Live" figure to weigh in on host Shane Gillis' controversial joke about women's athletic wear on Sunday, saying that he didn't "understand the kerfuffle" because the comedian wasn't being serious.

"I just didn't understand the kerfuffle — only because to me, I just saw it as what we call, I'll just say it, a joke! When you say jokes, you're not literally saying 'women are whores,' you are literally joking," Carvey said on the latest episode of his "Fly on the Wall" podcast with co-host David Spade. "Isn't that kind of the idea? No? Did I just get canceled?"

Carvey added that he'd bet the joke in question "destroyed" in comedy clubs before Gillis performed it from the "SNL" stage as part of his Oct. 10 monologue, but explained that the sketch series' Studio 8H was "not the right place" for it.

"Most of the audience is young women, so I think maybe that was not — it is very highly dressed up young women is the majority of the audience at 'SNL,'" Carvey said, hypothesizing why the bit landed with a thud.

Gillis come under fire this week after his guest hosting gig on "SNL," a program that previously fired him before he broke big on his own. He received blowback for a joke about women at the gym dressing like "whores."

"I haven't been to the gym in so long, I didn't know women just dress like whores now," Gillis quipped.

He added: "Look, I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I've seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they're like artificial bait-colored. And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combined at the butthole. And don't look, you're not allowed to look. For real, don't look because they are filming. I'm in the background of like 10 TikToks right now."

Celebrities and "SNL" alum like "Schitt's Creek" creator-star Dan Levy and former cast member Ego Nwodim ridiculed Gillis for the bit, while "Weekend Update" host and writer Michael Che was more reluctant to join the dogpile.

"That's comedy," Che said. "It's like, you think it's funny and some people don't."

Carvey and Spade appeared to fall more in line with Che's thinking on Sunday, with Spade adding that Gillis "knows that one's going to be a button-pusher, but he doesn't care."

"It's almost comical that there's people that say, 'Oh, don't make fun of Onlyfans. Don't make fun of strippers. These are sex workers, they need to be respected.' And everyone hates Sydney Sweeney. And it's like, what? Which one is it?" Spade said. "Let's all decide what we hate and don't, how about we just relax. Sometimes people just need to mind their biz. We don't need a comment on everything."

As far as whether or not the monologue is having a negative impact on Gillis, Spade said that "it actually helps him ultimately."

"I think he's that kind of Chappelle where he just does it and he walks away and then everyone fights over it," he said.

Watch Carvey and Spade's full "Fly on the Wall" episode in the video below.

articles.title: Revolut is down.
articles.summary:

articles.title: Some Google Home Speakers caught downloading hundreds of gigs of data
articles.summary: A bug impacting some Google Home Speakers is making them continuously download masses of data in the background.
articles.body: Some Google Home Speaker owners are currently experiencing an issue in which hundreds of gigabytes of data are being continuously downloaded to their device in the background. The bug, reported by 9to5Google and several Reddit users over the last week, may be caused by the speakers failing to correctly download and install a firmware update, with one Redditor finding that his device was consuming more than 200GB per day. Thankfully, Google is aware of the issue. In a statement to 9to5Google, the company said that “a fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.” Most of the reports are tied specifically to the new Google Home Speaker model, but it isn’t clear how widespread the issue is. We’ve reached out to Google to request more information about the cause and confirm impacted devices. My colleague Tom Warren confirmed that his own speaker is unaffected, and 9to5Google reports another Home Speaker in a different household downloaded just 2GB in the past month, compared to to 132GB used by an impacted device over the same period. A big concern for anyone with a limited data plan here is that the bug could quickly eat through the allotted limit, and they wouldn’t know unless they regularly check to see how much data their devices are using.

articles.title: Oura adds new fitness metrics to show how workouts impact your body | TechCrunch
articles.summary: While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors as the smart ring market gets more crowded.
articles.body:
As competition in the smart ring market escalates , Oura is introducing two new features to give people more insight into their workouts and how they impact their bodies. The company announced on Tuesday it’s rolling out Cardio Effort and VO₂ max metrics to expand workout tracking beyond exercise duration and heart rate zones.

While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors.

With Cardio Effort, users will be able to see how much a workout taxes their cardiovascular system. This measurement is aggregated over the week relative to each user’s individual baseline to provide more insights. Oura explained that this metric shifts users’ focus from “How many minutes did I move?” to “Am I maintaining my fitness, building it, or overdoing it?”

Since Cardio Effort accounts for both intensity and duration, a shorter, more intense workout can yield a similar score to a longer, less intense one, the company says.

Oura notes that the metric has two components: Workout Cardio Effort and Weekly Cardio Effort. The first metric evaluates the impact of an individual workout, while the latter aggregates effort into a weekly total, categorized as “Light,” “Fair,” “Maintaining,” “Building,” or “Reaching.”

Oura measures elevated heart rate relative to each member’s long-term resting heart rate, avoiding the variability associated with maximum-heart-rate estimates. Weekly effort levels are then determined using personalized ranges based on recent activity patterns.

Cardio Effort is rolling out to Oura Ring Gen3 and later models.

As for VO₂ max, the metric shows how workouts contribute to long-term fitness. It measures how effectively the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen during exercise. Previously, measuring VO₂ max typically required a lab test or a six-minute walking test. Oura can now estimate it passively using GPS-enabled workouts.

After completing five qualifying activities, users receive an initial VO2 Max estimate. Within the My Health Heart Hub, they can view their current VO2 Max estimate in ml/kg/min, their fitness category (Low, Fair, High, or Peak), how their estimate has changed over time, and when it was last updated. Users also receive insights highlighting meaningful changes in their VO2 Max or indicating when their estimate remains consistent.

VO₂ Max is launching in Oura Labs, the company’s hub for experimental features, for members with Gen3 and newer Oura Ring devices.

Oura says these two new features are designed to work together to show users how hard they’re working and how that effort is adding up over time.

articles.title: Turn membership cards into digital passes on your phone
articles.summary: Apple Wallet in iOS 27 lets you create digital passes from physical cards using a photo or screenshot, but not every card in your wallet qualifies.
articles.body: Take a look inside your wallet. There is a good chance at least one piece of plastic in there does little more than display a barcode. Maybe it is your library card. Perhaps it is a gym membership, grocery rewards card or another card you pull out every once in a while. Until now, getting some of those cards onto an iPhone could depend on whether the organization offered its own digital pass. Apple is changing that with iOS 27. The latest iPhone software lets you create your own pass in Apple Wallet from a physical card, photo or screenshot. Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel owners have similar options, which means you may be able to leave a few more plastic cards at home. Here is how to turn a membership card into a digital pass on all three phones. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. HOW TO SEARCH ANYTHING ON IPHONE, GALAXY AND PIXEL What's new with Apple Wallet in iOS 27? Apple added the ability to create your own passes in Wallet with iOS 27. This comes in handy when a membership or loyalty card has a barcode or QR code, but the organization never gave you an "Add to Apple Wallet" button. Apple specifically points to library cards and gym memberships as examples. If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone, you can create a pass from a photo or screenshot containing the barcode or QR code. Apple Intelligence recognizes the code and can give you the option to add it to Wallet. Apple Intelligence on iOS 27 requires a supported device, including the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 family and later compatible models. Availability can also depend on your language and region. However, Apple also gives you a manual way to create a pass directly inside Wallet. How to create an Apple Wallet pass from a photo or screenshot First, make sure the barcode or QR code is clearly visible. A blurry photo could make the code difficult for your iPhone to recognize or for a scanner to read later. On a compatible iPhone, Apple Intelligence can recognize the barcode or QR code in a photo or screenshot and offer to create a Wallet pass. On a compatible iPhone running iOS 27 or later: Pro tip: After you create the pass, you can tap View Original Photo to see the image you used. How to manually create a pass in Apple Wallet You can also build a pass yourself in iOS 27. This gives you another option when you want to add the information manually. How to edit a pass you created in Apple Wallet Once you've created a pass, you can customize its appearance or change the information it contains. You can also add or remove fields if you want different details displayed. HERE'S SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE How to add a membership card to Samsung Wallet Samsung Galaxy owners already have a similar option through Samsung Wallet. Samsung says almost any membership card with a barcode can be stored in the app. On a Galaxy phone running the latest available Samsung software: Samsung also supports participating memberships that are already built into Wallet. Once you need the card, open Samsung Wallet and select the membership. The barcode can then appear on your screen for a cashier or compatible reader to scan. Menu names can vary slightly depending on your Galaxy model and Samsung Wallet version. How to turn a membership card into a Google Wallet pass on Pixel Google Wallet can save passes from images when they contain a barcode or QR code. Google specifically lists library cards, gym passes and parking passes as examples. On a Google Pixel running the latest software: When you need the card, open Google Wallet and select the pass. You can then scan its barcode or QR code at the reader. Tip: Google also lets you return to the original image you used to create the pass. Open the pass and tap the More button in the upper-right corner to find the original image. You may also see Everything else under Add to Wallet . Google uses this option for creating other types of passes from a photo. Select Everything else , accept the consent terms if prompted, then take a photo or choose one from your phone. Google will preview the information it detects so you can review and manually edit it before tapping Add. What kinds of cards should you try? Start with cards whose main purpose is giving a business or organization a barcode or QR code to scan. A library card is an obvious candidate. Gym memberships and store loyalty cards may work well, too. Parking passes and other simple barcode-based credentials can also be good candidates, depending on how the organization verifies them. The easiest test is to look at the physical card. If the person behind the counter normally scans a static barcode or QR code printed on it, there is a reasonable chance a digital version can work. Keep the physical card until you have successfully tested the digital version. Some scanners may have trouble reading a phone display, and some organizations may require the original card. What these homemade digital passes cannot replace There is an important limit here. Creating a digital pass from a photograph does not turn every card in your wallet into an official digital credential. Do not assume you can photograph a driver's license, credit card, secure workplace badge or another sensitive credential and use the resulting image as an official replacement. Some digital credentials require verification from the organization that issued them. Payment cards also have separate security and enrollment requirements. Event tickets deserve extra caution. Many ticketing services now use barcodes that refresh or change to prevent fraud. A screenshot of one of those codes may fail at the gate. Whenever an issuer provides an official Add to Apple Wallet, Add to Google Wallet or Samsung Wallet option, use that instead. YOUR PHONE SAYS IT'S UPDATED. CHECK OTHER SETTINGS, TOO Kurt's key takeaways I like this iOS 27 addition because it fixes a surprisingly annoying limitation. I have had plenty of cards with perfectly usable barcodes that could not go into Apple Wallet simply because the organization behind them never created a digital pass. Now Apple is giving iPhone owners more control over that process. Samsung and Google already offer useful ways to accomplish something similar, so this is one of those rare phone features that can help you regardless of which of the big three you carry. I would start with the low-risk stuff. Put your library card or gym membership on your phone and see how it goes. If it saves you from carrying another card around every day, great. Just remember that a photo-based pass and an official digital credential are very different things. Your phone can replace more of your wallet than it used to, but I would not empty the whole thing yet. If your phone could replace every card in your wallet tomorrow, which physical card would you be most nervous about giving up for good? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: The Gospel according to Peter (Thiel)
articles.summary: We have Peter Thiel’s secret lectures about the Antichrist.
articles.body: It’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism, a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. EA is a utilitarian approach to charity premised on doing the most good for the most people over the longest time, and EA advocates see halting an AI-induced doomsday as critical to saving as many humans as possible. But EA has an important and equally apocalyptic rival in the crosscutting cosmologies of the tech titans — a strain of Christianity best represented by Peter Thiel, who believes EA will bring about the Antichrist. It’s an issue on which the billionaire techno-capitalist is a self-styled expert, and, somehow, Thiel has become America’s most provocative and visible Christian theologian. Thiel’s current fixation on the End of the World as We Know It is in theological language called eschatology, the study of the “last things.” His specific bête noire is the Antichrist, the villain of these end times scenarios. Thiel’s riffs on the Antichrist began a little over three years ago, first in a 2023 talk at the Catholic University of America but then, starting in 2025, only in closed-door, invitation-only, multipart lectures out of San Francisco. While that secrecy is frustrating for those of us interested in how uber-rich and politically powerful tech titans see the future of our world, it’s also rather savvy — no surprise from the guy who started hugely successful ventures like PayPal and Palantir. “It’s a pretty good marketing shtick if you want everybody to hear about something, not to let anybody in the room,” Thiel reportedly told one San Francisco audience last fall. In March, he traveled to Rome for another private, four-part series on the Antichrist. Taking his shtick to the doorstep of the Vatican was guaranteed to generate publicity, and it did. Months ago, recordings of Thiel’s lectures were leaked to The Verge. We have listened to and read transcripts of all four of these lectures, which provide a window into Thiel’s dizzying religious and sociocultural philosophy. He comes off as an intellectual magpie who somehow combines disparate elements into grave warnings against the AI and general “safetyism” that he claims precedes the Antichrist. “Peace and safety” — the slogan of the Antichrist, according to Thiel — trouble him throughout the lectures. In the first, he wonders if we’re headed toward World War III or Cold War II, and afterward, potentially, an unjust peace, the corollary to an unjust war: > Somehow, it’s very strange how the first Cold War from ’49 to ’89 ended. But it ended with roughly what I think of as a just peace. Where somehow you didn’t have a nuclear war. And somehow our side, which I think was more the good side, basically won. And you ended up not with a perfect peace, but more or less a just peace. And so if we have World War III, it will be an unjust war. If we have Cold War II, maybe it can end in a just peace or an unjust peace. > Reflecting on this material and thinking about it, it’s obviously not written in stone and there’s a lot of different ways this stuff can go. But I keep thinking that, if you had to put odds on it, aren’t the odds that we’re trending towards the fourth quadrant this time? The fourth possibility is that Cold War II will end an unjust peace. And it’s because the Antichrist talks about Armageddon nonstop. We’re all scared to death that we’re sleepwalking into Armageddon. And then because we know World War III will be an unjust war, that pushes us very hard towards peace at any price. > What I worry about in that sort of situation is you don’t think too hard about the details of the peace and it becomes much more likely that you get an unjust peace. This is, by the way, the slogan of the Antichrist: 1 Thessalonians 5:3. It’s “peace and safety,” the unjust peace. And then what Christ says in Matthew 24:6, the full verse: “And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, see that ye be not troubled.” If you’re too troubled, will we always end up with very unjust peace? Or something like this. We are publishing an analysis of these lectures now because Thiel published a version of these same ideas in the conservative religious journal First Things in July. You can read along for yourself. Titled “The Pope and the Antichrist,” the essay fills in the huge gaps in Thiel’s thinking and allows us to better understand his ideas, such as they are. The bottom line is that after sifting through all of the arcane references and esoteric exegesis, it turns out that Thiel — a Protestant who likes to describe himself as a “heterodox Christian” — offers a fairly standard-issue American evangelical worldview, and a rather fundamentalist one at that. He’s less a coherent religious thinker than a repackager of recognizable ideas — dressing them up in the rhetoric of a tech nerd turned theological hobbyist — which he uses to promote his own ideology. He reads everything from the Bible to pre-papal writings of a future pope to Robert Hugh Benson’s 1907 novel Lord of the World to semi-obscure Scottish poetry with an eye toward his own, sometimes shockingly literal interpretation of the Antichrist’s arrival (ideally, he should make his mark, as it were, more quickly than Jesus, who died at 33 and a few months — although Thiel allows in his third lecture that perhaps “in our gerontocracy, 66 is the new 33”). While his mashup of religious concepts and authoritative assertions on dubious interpretations make him sound like an undergrad who just took his first philosophy class and then a few too many hits on the bong, the goal of his eschatology is the same as every apocalyptic visionary: to divide the world between the saved and the damned. And Thiel is, clearly, one of the righteous. It’s notable here that Thiel is coming from the heart of what is arguably America’s latest, and most unexpected, religious revival — one concentrated among the Silicon Valley elite, like the ACTS 17 Collective, which is a reference to St. Paul’s preaching to the Greek pagans in the Acts of the Apostles and an acronym for “Acknowledging Christ in Technology and Society.” But that movement presents an upbeat message of self-improvement through Jesus, the kind that the clean-and-fit Bay Area crowd tends to embrace. Thiel’s worldview is quite unusual for Silicon Valley, and perhaps especially unexpected for a gay German billionaire; he’s right at home in the US tradition of apocalypticism. The key to Thiel’s theological vision comes at the very opening of his most recent First Things essay, and it is his fixation on, and fear of, the Antichrist. The Antichrist has traditionally been associated with, as Thiel himself put it elsewhere, “an evil king or tyrant or anti-messiah who appears in the end times.” That is true, though Thiel says that the Antichrist interests him “mostly because nobody else is talking about it.” That would be news to anybody with even a passing familiarity with American Christianity. In fact, the Antichrist and eschatology are arguably the central religious impulse running through American Christianity, and that focus distinguishes the US from most other churches and cultures around the globe. In America, biblical teachings tend to jump from the Ten Commandments at the beginning of the Old Testament to the Book of Revelation at the end of the New Testament. The Gospels, the Beatitudes, all that provides the key teachings of Jesus Christ is a footnote. [Image: The enthusiasm for the end of the world has been fueled in large part by the series of sweeping revivals, or “Great Awakenings,” that have marked American religious history from the Colonial era up through the 1800s and, some would say, on into the 20th century. These revivals focused not only on personal conversion but on dark warnings about the “end times” as foretold in the New Testament, when Christ would return to gather believers up to Heaven and those who remained would be stuck facing various tribulations on their own. For American Christians especially, the quest to save souls from eternal damnation was increasingly driven by the fear that the Second Coming was imminent, so you’d better repent now. New apocalyptic movements and sects and cults continued to flourish, from those early tent revivals through the more slickly branded televangelists and, later, the enormously popular Left Behind series of novels in the 1990s. Forecasters variously took snippets in the Book of Daniel and other prophets in the Hebrew Bible and joined them with the often phantasmagoric array of visions from the Book of Revelation, and eventually what had been a confusing jumble of end times scenarios solidified into a widely accepted timeline: increasing natural and human-made disasters, the Second Coming of Jesus, aka the Rapture of true believers, followed by the rise of the Antichrist and seven years of the Great Tribulation on Earth, ending with a final battle between good and evil and a thousand years of peace. --- Peter Thiel on Bill Gates “One of my friends was telling me that I should not pass up on the opportunity to tell those people in San Francisco that Bill Gates is the Antichrist. I will concede that he is certainly a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde-type character. The public Mr. Rogers, the neighborhood character — but I saw the Mr. Hyde version about a year ago, where it was just a nonstop Tourette’s, yelling swear words, almost incomprehensible what was going on. Certainly, of course, there are a lot of people who are wannabe Antichrists. They sort of want peace and safety. [He] definitely wants a Nobel Peace Prize. He would give his soul for that, no question about it.” Eliezer Yudkowsky “There is another book — I haven’t been able to get a copy of it because it’s coming out tomorrow, but we sort of downloaded it — that fits this thesis even better. It’s from the East Bay rationalist Eliezer Yudkowsky. I’m embarrassed about all the ways I was once affiliated with these various people and how deranged and crazy they’ve all gone. It started with these Baconian aspirations of transformative technology: We’re going to build it, it’s going to change the world. And then it’s somehow ended in some sort of blackpilled thing that’s probably more depressed and more Luddite than Greta.” Greta Thunberg “I think one of the ways these things always get reported is I denounce Greta as an Antichrist. And I want to be very clear, Greta is not, I mean, she’s maybe sort of a type or a shadow of an Antichrist of the sort that would be tempting, but I don’t want to flatter her too much.” Marc Andreessen “It’s not Andreessen, by the way. I think Andreessen is not the Antichrist. Because, you know, the Antichrist is popular.” --- Phew. Now enter Peter Thiel. He is in effect the latest in a long line of apocalypticists, though his own spin is that anxieties over strange new technologies like AI will prompt demands for greater regulation and that would be a grave, almost apocalyptic, mistake. Given the latest warnings from AI leaders themselves that the new technology could risk human extinction within a decade, Thiel’s concerns run counter to what you’d expect from an apocalypticist. Thiel’s theological justification for criticizing this instinct toward what he derides as “safetyism” rests on a verse in St. Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians in which the apostle warns that many will promote “peace and safety” to lull people into a false sense of security and then POOF, Jesus returns and the Antichrist appears and unbelievers are doomed. Thiel identifies promoters of this kind of peace and safety with a “restraining” force that will be a sign of the coming of the Antichrist and which will eventually pave the way for the Antichrist. He has pointed to Anthony Fauci as one example of such a “restrainer.” And now the apostles of effective altruism, with their concern for protecting as many people as possible, are in Thiel’s sights. Thiel uses the original Greek term for “the restrainer,” katechon, because of course he does. Deploying arcane terms is part of the mystery that gives apocalypticism its allure, and prophets their power. So who is actually the Antichrist? Thiel at one point dismissed such speculations as “down-market” behavior, but he himself cannot resist weighing in. Viewing the Roman pontiff as the Antichrist or a collaborator with the Antichrist is a standard trope of end times theology, and in his First Things essay Thiel follows that tradition by suggesting that the late Pope Francis could have been the Antichrist. In previously leaked snippets of Thiel’s talks he has accused the current American pope, Leo XIV, of being a “Chinese communist agent” or, more recently, Beijing’s “useful idiot,” because he wants to regulate AI — all very Antichrist-adjacent behavior. Thiel has a somewhat unusual relationship to the Catholic Church. True to the more anti-papist strains of his tradition, he worries that Pope Leo XIV is a “woke American pope” who will join with American liberals to create a tyrannical “Caesaro-Papist fusion.” At the same time, the German-born Thiel’s record-breaking financial support propelled JD Vance, a relatively recent Catholic convert, to the US Senate and now a heartbeat away from the presidency. Thiel has also made a little-known Catholic literary theorist from France, René Girard, a spiritual guide for America’s political right — though only by completely inverting Girard’s famous teaching about the scapegoat mechanism by which a society eases internal divisions by blaming a single person or subgroup of people for their problems. Thiel’s latest essay is also unusual, or inventive, in that rather than denouncing the papacy as the Whore of Babylon — a traditional fundamentalist Protestant trope drawn from a stark image in Revelation 17 — he tries to co-opt one pope, the late Benedict XVI, into his very American and Protestant worldview and against the papacy and the Catholic Church itself. “I did not come to Rome to try to be more Catholic than the pope, but I did hope, even as a Protestant, to be more Catholic than the average Catholic,” Thiel says. His aim is to use Benedict — who resigned as pope in 2013 and died in seclusion in the Vatican in 2022 — as the one Catholic leader who understood the imminent threat of the Antichrist and the end times, the one Catholic who got it right. Granted, Benedict is the one pope who provides Thiel with the kind of opening, however tiny, that Thiel could run with. Benedict was “a decided Augustinian,” as he wrote during his earlier days as Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, and he shared St. Augustine’s rather pessimistic view of humankind. Thiel spends much time on the young Ratzinger’s dissertation on St. Bonaventure’s theology of history — a recondite topic in which the 13th-century Italian Franciscan rebutted the odd apocalyptic writings of Joachim of Fiore, an Italian abbot who lived a century before St. Bonaventure. Thiel somehow reads Ratzinger’s endorsement of Bonaventure over Joachim of Fiore as a sign that Ratzinger saw the apocalypse coming rather than what Ratzinger actually wrote and meant. In his third lecture Thiel extrapolates wildly on this theme from a quote within a footnote, saying: > The TL;DR: My belief is that Benedict literally thought that the historic falling away from the church during his papacy was a sign of the end times. > Is there evidence for this? There’s all sorts of subtle hints. Writing the 1959 professorial dissertation on Bonaventure, he uses all this colorful language on the Antichrist, the Whore of Babylon. What does one make of this? In a footnote, it’s sort of the most cryptic, esoteric way to write it. Not in his own words but quoting another professor, Ratzinger wrote — obviously before he’s Pope — quoting this other professor: “In the case of Bonaventure, we see how difficult it is to succeed in placing the proper limits on apocalyptic images. Apocalyptic images are like a torrent of water that overflows the banks and it’s difficult to keep in bounds. And regardless of all efforts to mollify the imagery, the apocalyptic tone predominates. Even a Mozart cannot make a trumpet forget to sound like a trumpet.” So it’s sort of like you are saying, if you think about this stuff, you can never, ever talk about it. If you talk about it even one peep, it will dominate everything and you can’t say anything else. The proof that future Pope Benedict was as focused on the literal end times as Thiel? That he would never talk about it, of course. What Ratzinger actually wanted was to avoid the idea that humanity could bring peace and justice to this world through our own efforts — a preview of his decadeslong campaign against what he saw as Marxist-influenced liberation theology, not on behalf of the Antichrist. Yet Thiel continues to pick out various comments on eschatology — “breadcrumbs,” Thiel calls them — from Ratzinger’s lectures and writings as the decades progressed and Ratzinger’s own theological vision admittedly grew darker and more conservative. He interprets Benedict’s resignation from the papacy — unprecedented in modern times — as one of Benedict’s “winks and hints” that the Antichrist is coming. This ventriloquizing is as bizarre as it is morbid, but Thiel is convinced that when it comes to talking about the Antichrist “these apocalyptic paroxysms make Benedict sound like a fire-and-brimstone Southern Baptist.” That comment shows Thiel’s basic problem, which is that he wants to view Roman Catholicism through an Evangelical Protestant lens that sees the end times as a global apocalypse where the “saved” will be rescued — and confirmed in their righteousness. Ratzinger, and later as Pope Benedict, was a thoroughgoing Catholic churchman who was less concerned about the end of time than he was “anxious about the end of a historical era of the Catholic Church,” as the Italian theologian Marcello Neri put it. Ratzinger saw Catholic liberals who would dilute church doctrine and dogma as the apocalyptic threat, and it’s a threat to the Catholic Church, not the planet. History will go on, Ratzinger believed. It’s the church’s fate that’s less certain, thanks to infiltration by modernist currents. Thiel is making a category error that undermines his entire argument. It’s typical Thiel. At the end of the day, and of his essay, Thiel’s grandiose language and project is shown to be a rather ordinary ideological one. “Thiel is above all a political theologian operating at the very heart of the Silicon Valley ecosystem,” the Italian Franciscan Paolo Benanti wrote in a sharp riposte to Thiel’s Rome talks. As Benanti explains, this ideology includes the “pathological radicalization” of a handful of Western values — “competition, technology, the individual” — resulting in outcomes “radically divergent from the common democratic project.” Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor elaborate on that theme in their new book, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World. [Image: If liberals want to “immanentize the eschaton,” as William F. Buckley once put it, by focusing on doing good in this life instead of being anxious about the world to come, conservatives tend to focus on personal salvation ahead of the apocalypse. That end times theology is a perfect match for them because it tends toward a libertarian ethos like Thiel’s; Jesus is coming back soon, let’s not get bogged down in overregulating or overthinking. “We moralize way too much,” as Thiel said in a podcast last month with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner. “If you’re evil, you’re at least competent. And if you’re evil, you’re not bad, and therefore you’re actually maybe kind of good because you’re at least getting something done.” Instead, Thiel suggests, let’s make hay — meaning, bushels of money — while the sun shines. Climate anxiety? Your worries about the future show a lack of faith! That’s why, in addition to the previous pope and the effective altruism movement, Thiel has also been reported as suggesting climate change activist Greta Thunberg might be the Antichrist. Or maybe, he suggests in one lecture, it’s the system that’s the real Antichrist — specifically the financial regulatory system. > The Book of Revelation tells us, sort of, the Antichrist will abolish financial freedom. Revelation 13:16–17: “He causes all, both great and small, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand or in their foreheads, that no man might buy or sell save that he had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.” > There’s this whole constellation of things, where over the last 25 years — this uneventful, Groundhog Day 21st century since 2000 — under cover of relative peace and safety, an incredible machinery of tax treaties, financial surveillance, and sanctions architecture has been constructed. And all these tech fortunes are downstream of this vast system. You have the illusion of power and autonomy, but you have this sense it could be taken away at any moment. It’s become quite difficult to hide one’s money. He admits that “this Antichrist-like system, this machinery” moves at a different speed than a human Antichrist (who, again, should probably be 33.5 or younger), but insists it was set up “not overnight but relatively quickly, and there’s a feeling it could be activated at the flip of a switch.” If that all seems like a definition of the Antichrist that only a billionaire could love, he assures his listeners it’s more than that. And then, of course, it’s not just a financial system. It’s also, in some sense, an ideological system. The Antichrist won’t stop just at money. Money is not enough to stop the Antichrist and follows that he wants something more from you. It’s also, per Thiel, the International Criminal Court and the way it has spooked Vladimir Putin, Benjamin Netanyahu, and erstwhile members of the George W. Bush administration, and it’s Germany’s strict laws around Nazi symbolism and libel online, and it’s Australian age verification laws, which all cobble together into a vision of the end of days that so transfixes him. It’s not exactly fire and brimstone, but to Thiel, it is. For all of Peter Thiel’s prominence and brilliance — Vance called him “the smartest man I’ve ever met” — his spiritual preoccupations are ultimately quite mainstream. Vance recently spent part of a long podcast with a popular Evangelical influencer talking about the End Times and the Antichrist. It blew the mind of most Catholics, but as Vance’s friend conservative Christian commentator Rod Dreher said, this is “a very, very common belief.” These beliefs are also very representative of an increasingly DIY religious culture in America that is disconnected from traditional practices and flesh-and-blood congregations. When it comes to religion, seemingly everyone now does their own research and generates their own social media ministry. The difference is that Thiel is an uber-wealthy influencer with political power. The theological thrifting by which he has sewn together his own apocalyptic vision would at one level be seen as quirky but innocent if not for the fact that he is using that vision to set himself up as a godlike judge between the saved and the damned — one might almost say a kind of Antichrist. That’s what eschatology has always done, but few apocalyptic preachers have wielded the kind of power Peter Thiel does, and he doesn’t seem to view many of us outside his circle as worthy of salvation. Additional reporting by Tina Nguyen

articles.title: Arturia’s MiniFreak 49 makes its Freak synths more professional
articles.summary: The MiniFreak 49 adds full-sized semi-weighted keys and proper pitch and mod wheels to the Freak lineup.
articles.body: Arturia is adding to its Freak line of proudly weird digital synths with the MiniFreak 49. Under the hood, it’s almost identical to the current MiniFreak, but it adds a number of more professional features and some interface improvements. The most noticeable change is that, rather than the MiniFreak’s 37 minikeys or the MicroFreak’s 25 “key” touchplate, the MiniFreak 49 has (as you may have guessed) 49 full-sized, semi-weighted keys. Though it’s somewhat disappointing that they feature only mono aftertouch instead of polyphonic aftertouch. It also trades the touchstrips of the other Freak instruments for proper aluminum pitch and mod wheels. The MiniFreak 49 also has a larger LCD than its siblings and dedicated controls for its two sound engines, so you don’t have to switch between them. Like the MiniFreak, it offers over 30 digital oscillator types, each with analog filters. It also adds audio-rate filter FM for even freakier sounds and has 256MB of storage for user samples and wavetables, which were just added to the original MiniFreak in a firmware update last month. Lastly, there’s a new XYZ touchpad that not only replaces the mod matrix’s intuitive but slow knob-based interface, but also adds performance features and speeds up preset browsing. You can swipe through presets, control macros, manipulate the filter, and more. MiniFreak 49 is available now with an MSRP of $849, though the street price is likely to be lower.

articles.title: Pioneer’s retro stereo brings modern features to vintage cars.
articles.summary:
The company’s new Heritage Collection is targeted at classic car collectors wanting modern stereo features like Bluetooth and support for HD Radio and SiriusXM while also preserving the vintage look of their vehicles. The $499 SXT-C10PS head unit and matching $299 TS-X40SXT speakers are both available for preorder now.

articles.title: Cat Deeley begins ‘massive renovation’ of new home with brother’s help after split from Patrick Kielty; ex-couple’s Hampstead house listed for £5 million after £250,000 price cut
articles.summary: This Morning presenter Cat Deeley has revealed that she is undertaking a “massive renovation” of her new house following her separation from Irish
articles.body: This Morning presenter Cat Deeley has revealed that she is undertaking a “massive renovation” of her new house following her separation from Irish television presenter Patrick Kielty. The 49-year-old presenter, who split from Patrick, 55, last July, said she is taking on the ambitious project independently, with help from her brother.In an interview with Closer magazine, Cat opened up about the renovation and explained why she enjoys taking on challenges that push her out of her comfort zone.“I'm doing a big renovation, which is a massive project, and my brother is helping me do it,” she said.“I like doing things that scare me a little bit.“I always feel like if an opportunity comes up or there's something life-changing that you want to do, if you feel a little bit scared and you're approaching it with a little trepidation then you should probably do it.”Cat did not reveal the location of her new property or share further details about the project.Cat Deeley and Patrick Kielty’s £5 million Hampstead home up for saleCat’s latest renovation project comes after the extensive redevelopment of the Hampstead home she purchased with Patrick in 2022. The former couple reportedly paid £4.9 million for the derelict 1950s property in north London, which they had planned to transform into their forever home.However, the ambitious renovation reportedly placed additional stress on their marriage. With Patrick working in Ireland and Cat presenting This Morning in London, managing the extensive redevelopment alongside their professional commitments proved challenging.Cat had previously documented the renovation on social media, offering followers a glimpse into the scale of the work involved.In a video shared in February 2024, she candidly admitted: “I'm not going to lie, I got a bit of a shock today. Not much house, lots of air.”The plans for the property included creating a grand entrance hall, removing the mezzanine floor in the living room and extending the bedrooms and terrace.Following their separation, the extensive renovation was halted, with the project becoming a significant undertaking to manage individually.The Hampstead property is now on the market with Savills for £5 million, after its asking price was reportedly reduced by £250,000 this summer.Cat and Patrick announced their separation last July after years together. The former couple share two sons, Milo, 10, and James, eight.Despite the changes in her personal life, Cat appears ready to embrace a new chapter, taking on a major property project of her own.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.
